sections.facts: Frank Anthony Public School is a recognised unaided minority school within the meaning of Sections 2(x) read with 2(e), 2(o), and 2(t) of the Delhi School Education Act. In the matter of emoluments and conditions of service, such as leave, teachers and employees of the school lag far behind those of Government schools, and several other conditions of service also compare unfavourably. But for Section 12, if Sections 8 to 11 were applicable, they would be at least as well off as their counterparts in Government schools. Sometime after the filing of the writ petition, on May 9, 1986, during the daily break between 10:00 A.M. and 10:40 A.M., the teaching staff (except one or two on duty) and Class IV staff took out a silent march without speeches, slogan shouting, violence, or disruption of studies, and classes resumed normally. Despite a warning notice issued by the principal on April 10, 1986, a similar silent march was taken out on April 10, 1986. Consequently, the management issued suspension orders against four staff members (Mrs. Malik, Mrs. Dhar, Mrs. Balman, and Mr. Bush). The petitioner association challenged these suspension orders and sought a stay of their operation in the writ petition.
sections.statute: Chapter IV of the Delhi School Education Act, comprising Sections 8 to 12, deals with the 'Terms and conditions of service of employees of recognised private schools.' Section 10(1) requires that the scales of pay and allowances, medical facilities, pension, gratuity, provident fund, and other prescribed benefits of employees of a recognised private school shall not be less than those of employees of corresponding status in schools run by the appropriate authority. Section 12 provides that 'Nothing contained in this Chapter shall apply to an unaided minority school.' Chapter V, comprising Sections 13 to 15, contains provisions applicable to unaided minority schools, including Section 13 enabling the Administrator to make regulations regarding minimum qualifications for recruitment. The effect of Section 12 is to make Sections 8, 9, 10, and 11 inapplicable to unaided minority schools regarding Administrator's service rules, prior approval of the Director for dismissal/removal/reduction in rank/termination, appeals against such orders, approvals for suspension, and parity of pay scales and allowances.
sections.argument: The petitioner association filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking equalisation of pay scales and service conditions with those of Government school counterparts and a declaration that Section 12 of the Act is void and unconstitutional as offending Articles 14, 21, and 23 of the Constitution. In response to the Rule Nisi, the respondents contended that: (i) the classification made by Section 12 was perfectly valid; (ii) but for Section 12, Sections 8 to 11 would interfere with the right guaranteed by Article 30 of the Constitution to religious and linguistic minorities to administer educational institutions of their choice; (iii) the school was an institution of great repute whose excellence spoke for itself and did not necessitate regulation by any other authority; (iv) the scale of fees had to be kept low to remain within reach of ordinary people, which prevented payment of higher salaries and allowances; and (v) if Section 12 were struck down and the management compelled to pay Government-scale salaries, the school would have to be closed down.
sections.analysis: There is a general and broad consensus that the right guaranteed to religious and linguistic minorities by Article 30(1) of the Constitution is to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The extent of this right is determined with reference to making the institutions effective vehicles of education, and regulatory measures designed towards this goal do not impinge upon Article 30(1) so long as they do not nullify the right of management in substantial measure. As established in In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957, conditions cannot be imposed that force the surrender of Article 30(1) rights, nor does the right depend on receipt of aid. The excellence of instruction directly depends on the quality and contentment of the teachers; thus, service conditions prescribing minimum qualifications, pay scales, allowances, and living standards to prevent oppression or exploitation are permissible regulations. Therefore, Section 10 is a permissible regulation aimed at excellence and does not detract from Article 30(1). Section 8(1) is innocuous. Section 8(2), which requires prior approval of the Director for dismissal, removal, reduction in rank, or termination, interferes with minority management rights and is objectionable. However, Section 8(3) provides a reasonable and limited right of appeal to an independent judicial Tribunal. Sections 8(4) and 8(5) provide a sound safeguard against abuse by requiring approval within 15 days while preserving the right to order immediate suspension for gross misconduct. Section 9 is innocuous since Section 14 applies similar provisions. Sections 8(1), 8(3), 8(4), 8(5), 9, and 11 do not encroach upon minority administration rights, as also demonstrated by Parliament applying Chapter IV to aided minority institutions without offending Article 30(1).
sections.judgement: The Supreme Court allowed the writ petition, holding that Section 12 of the Delhi School Education Act, which makes the provisions of Chapter IV inapplicable to unaided minority schools, is discriminatory and void not only because it makes Section 10 inapplicable, but also because it makes Sections 8(1), 8(3), 8(4), 8(5), 9, and 11 inapplicable to unaided minority institutions. Section 8(2), however, interferes with the right of minorities to administer educational institutions and is inapplicable to minority institutions.
